senses: Synonym of ladybird.
ety: From lady + bug, the “lady” here referring to Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus. Compare German Marienkäfer, Danish mariehøne, Latvian mārīte, Macedonian бубамара (bubamara) and Spanish mariquita.

senses: A company operating in only one industry or line of business; often specifically a bank specializing in credit card issuance.
A font line of consistent width, as occurs when imitating pencil script.
A length of monofilament line, used for culturing forms of seaweed.
A type of composing machine in which each line of type is cast as a single slug.
A single spectrum line.
examples: The other leading monolines in 2002 were Capital One and Providian.
A module consists of 21 monolines; a monoline on the other hand is 20 feet (6 m) long and consists of a nylon line plus 3 stakes— 2 at both ends and one at the middle— and 30 plants.
With the straight matter being set on the linotype or monoline, the hand compositor was left with what he claimed was the most 'skilled' part of his old work.

senses: The solid piston of a force pump; the instrument by which water is forced in a pump.
A small hand pump for sinking pits, draining cellars, etc.
A bell-shaped lidded pot for growing rhubarb, used to limit photosynthesis by excluding light, encouraging early-season growth and blanched stems.
Having the psychological condition of egomania.
The quality or state of being unitary.
examples: In this section, we shall prove the gauge invariance and unitarity of the physical S-matrix in quantum electrodynamics, to all orders in the renormalized perturbation theory.

senses: The state of living near something; proximity, closeness.
ety: From Old French visnage, respelled to more closer match its Latin source vīcīnus (“neighbor”). By surface analysis, vicine + -age.

senses: The dignity, estate, term, or jurisdiction of an abbot or abbess.
ety: From Middle English abbathie, from Late Latin abbātia, from abbās, abbātis (“abbot”). Doublet of abbey and Opatija.

senses: The use of ultrasound to form images of underwater structures.
A form of fine-grained quartz that is nearly transparent or has a milky translucence; it fractures conchoidally.
ety: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).

senses: One who plays a banjo.
Characterised by being timorous or afraid.
ety: Back-formation from scaredy-cat, equivalent to scared + -y.
examples: Prescott's sister calls him a scaredy kitten because he's afraid of the dark.

senses: Containing wine.
Of the colour of red wine.
Of a specific color among several that represent red wine.
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin vinaceus, from Latin vinum.

senses: A book in which laws are codified.
A textbook on some aspect of law.
ety: Perhaps from Middle English *lawe-bok, from Old Norse lǫgbók (“lawbook”), otherwise, from law + book. Compare Middle English laȝheboc.

senses: Any mechanical device, manufactured using nanotechnology, having a scale measured in nanometres.
Synonym of ontogenesis.
From or relating to a psychrometer.
A square chamber that serves as the section of an industrial fishing net from which captured fish can easily be moved to a fishing boat.
ety: From Middle English spiller, from spill + -er.

senses: The normal process by which bone is formed.
The process of becoming set in one's ways or beliefs; rigid conventionality.
ety: From Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + -ification. Recorded earlier than ossify.

senses: A group of martens.
ety: From Middle English richesse, from Old French richese, richece.

senses: The process of becoming mature.
ety: From Middle English maturacioun, from Middle French maturation, from Latin maturatio. By surface analysis, mature + -ation.

senses: To furnish with accessories.
To wear or to choose accessories.
ety: From accessory + -ize. First attested in 1939 in American English.

senses: Covered with mud.
A hitchhiker.
An onsetter.
A prejudiced attitude about human height that often results in discrimination, based on the belief that unusually short or tall people are inferior and undesirable.
examples: It is obvious that the dimensions of inequality could be extended to include a great many differences such as heightism where people who are taller are superior to people who are shorter, and so forth.
There might be reinforcement of already harmful social evils such as heightism and racism.
Given this background, how can dwarfs, beset by beautyism, heightism, and a succession of slights, move toward positive body images and self-esteem?

senses: One who laps liquid, who takes liquid in with the tongue.
Something (especially a race) that has a stated number of laps.
One who wraps or folds.
A mechanism that overlaps material to make it thicker; a lapping cylinder or lapping machine.
One who files something.
Any of several breeds of dog.
The act of collineating; collimation.
ety: From Latin collineare to direct in a straight line. See collimation.

senses: To make democratic.
To broaden access to (something), especially for the sake of egalitarianism.
ety: From French démocratiser. By surface analysis, democrat(ic) + -ize.

senses: Plasticine; modelling clay.
ety: From Irish marla, from Middle English marle. Doublet of marl.
examples: Miss Carney handed us out blank paper and marla, old plasticine with the colours all rolled together into brown.
As she sits and plays with Damien, she feels her legs start to tremble from the effort. Her knees seem to disappear. Plasticine legs, she says to Damien. Old marla legs.

senses: One skilled in the theory or construction of machines.
One skilled in building, using, or repairing machines, or who makes machines or tools.
One skilled in mechanics.
A machinist.
A scientifically trained practitioner.
examples: To build such a device will require an expert mechanician.
The Cotton-Gin is a machine to separate the seeds from cotton, invented by that celebrated mechanician, E. Whitney. -- from the 1828 Webster's Dictionary.
The Yankees, the first mechanicians in the world, are engineers—just as the Italians are musicians and the Germans metaphysicians—by right of birth.

senses: California white oak (Quercus lobata).
Nothofagus obliqua (syn. Lophozonia obliqua); noble beech.
Covered in vomit.
Prone to sickness; easily becoming ill; (somewhat) sick.
examples: Also consider how easy is it to clean with a sicky baby; can all of the cover and straps go in the washing machine or is it wipe clean only?
I started off with 18 sleepsuits, but got through them in 24 hours when she was sicky.
DS was sicky when still in a moses basket, but had pretty much grown out of it by the time he was in a cot.

senses: Of a colour: from which some wavelengths have been removed.
The process of seeking employment
examples: Jobseekers are entitled to personalised jobsearch planning and job-matching, with direct access to vacancies.

senses: The traditional time, in the late afternoon, for serving tea (the meal).
ety: From tea + time. Compare Saterland Frisian Teetied (“teatime”), West Frisian teetiid (“teatime”), Dutch theetijd (“teatime”), German Teezeit (“teatime”), Danish tetid (“teatime”), Swedish tetid (“teatime”), Icelandic tetími (“teatime”).

senses: Any of many small crustaceans, of the class Ostracoda, that resemble a shrimp enclosed in a bivalve shell.
ety: From Ancient Greek ὀστρακώδης (ostrakṓdēs, “covered with shell”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot; shell”); compare translingual Ostracoda.
examples: Considering all the ecological data, there seems to be an evolution in the associations of ostracods throughout time.
This study has also shown that the fifth limb is most probably of thoracic origin and hence ostracods have only one pair of maxillae.
A number of parasites and epibionts have been reported from freshwater ostracods, including cestodes, protozoans, helminthes, peritrichs, and acanthocephalans (Griffits and Evans 1994).

senses: A 360-degree theatre, a circular room where the viewer sits or stands in the center and films are projected on the walls on all sides.
examples: The panarama's like being inside a videodrome of revolving landscapes by Thomas Moran.
At the moment there are two types of VR: one which one can experience via a stereohelmet, a glove and even a complete dress (cybersuit), and one which one can experience in a videodrome.
It was a seven story building where you first had to "buy time" in order to use over 50 facilities ranging from a videodrome to a swimming pool.

senses: Non-Oxford British spelling of visualize.
ety: From visual + -ise (a variant of -ize (suffix forming verbs denoting the doing or making of what is denoted by the adjectives or nouns to which it is attached)).
examples: The humanitarian, frequently ignoring hard reality, visualises one cosmopolitan community where justice and social sympathy measured in terms of some one set of units reign supreme.
Possible developments such as electric or diesel suburban services may be visualised when the town has grown sufficiently to justify them.

senses: The act or process of fluidizing.
